text: 🇲🇽✊ "It is not the same, 5% of 80 pesos as 5% of 248." — Octavio Romero Oropeza, Director of Infonavit, Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Chiapas Employers pay 5% of each worker's wage into Infonavit's housing fund. López Obrador took the daily minimum wage from 80 to 248 pesos; Sheinbaum followed with raises of 12% and 13%. Romero said the fund held 140 billion pesos when López Obrador arrived, 780 billion when he left, and holds 1.14 trillion today. That money now finances construction directly, so builders no longer load bank interest into the price. With federal, state and municipal fee waivers and builders accepting smaller margins, homes worth over 1.2 million pesos — at least 60 m², two bedrooms — are delivered for a little over half their cost to workers earning 1 to 2.9 minimum wages.

🇲🇽✊ "What governments do, if we are good governments, is help the people. The effort is yours. We facilitate, we help fulfill something that is a right of the people of Mexico: access to housing, access to education, access to health, a good wage, being able to open a small business. That is what governments that love the people do. And if there is one thing that characterizes the governments of the Fourth Transformation, it is that we love the people of Mexico." — Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Chiapas On November 8 she handed over 55 Infonavit apartments at the Los Poetas housing development in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, plus 311 Fovissste mortgage-settlement certificates. The Vivienda para el Bienestar program aims at 1.8 million homes for low-income families; 5 million families have had their Infonavit or Fovissste debts restructured. Counting deeds and new credits, she said 12 million families will benefit in total.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>US Tariffs Hit Cars That Are 40% American-Made</u>

US imports of passenger cars from Mexico fell 20% in January–July 2026 compared with the same period of 2024, even as total imports from Mexico rose nearly 24%, El Economista reports. CSIS researcher Diego Marroquín Bitar told the US International Trade Commission that "Mexican vehicles incorporate, on average, around 40% US components," far more than cars from other markets. He warned that tightening T-MEC rules of origin "would start raising costs and displacing production outside North America."

🇲🇽🚆 <u>Delfina Gómez Puts Edomex Highway Concessionaires on Notice</u>

State of Mexico Governor Delfina Gómez is reviewing every highway concession granted under public-private partnership (APP) and long-term service (PPS) contracts. Companies that failed to maintain their roads will lose them. Concessionaires let Periférico Norte, Periférico Oriente, Paseo Tollocan and Avenida Las Torres fall apart, so the state's own road agency had to step in. It has already rehabilitated 1,638 km in the biggest road-rescue program in four decades.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>38 Raids, 32 Arrests: Anti-Extortion Strategy Hits Edomex and CDMX</u>

Federal and state forces carried out 38 raids in the State of Mexico and Mexico City under the National Strategy Against Extortion. They arrested 32 people, including three alleged leaders of groups running extortion, drug dealing, arms trafficking, property seizures and illegal LP gas sales. In Ecatepec, one of them ran his operation behind the front of a "union."

🇲🇽⚖️ <u>Supreme Court and Judicial Workers Reach a Deal: No Punitive Evaluations</u>

Judicial workers staged stoppages in at least 17 states. Mexico's Supreme Court, the Judicial Administration Body (OAJ) and the federal judiciary's unions then agreed that performance reviews under agreement AG-POAJ-025/2026 will carry no sanctions and can't be used to remove anyone from their post. Judges also lose the power to order surprise evaluations of their staff. Federal courts reopen as normal on Monday, November 9.

🇲🇽💵 <u>Higher Wages, More on the Plate: Mexico's Meat Consumption Up 27%</u>

Mexico has logged five straight years of rising meat consumption, from 9.06 million tons in 2020 to 11.55 million in 2025. That's a 27% jump. And it's the producers themselves giving the credit: minimum-wage policy, social programs, the anti-inflation package (PACIC) and remittances. Between January and October 2026, consumer chicken prices fell 4.5% and pork 2.8%.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>Citi: Mexico Set to Win From the AI Boom</u>

Citi Research's "LatAm Poised for Take-Off" report names Mexico one of the main winners of North America's supply-chain reshuffle: it has gained share of US imports and locked in its place as Washington's No. 1 trading partner, El Economista reports. The driver is AI. Mexican exports of CPUs, assembled from Taiwanese and other Asian parts and shipped north, have been a major source of that gain. Citi's caveat: a pipeline of investment projects is waiting for clarity on the T-MEC review.
banner: CITI: MEXICO WINS FROM AI BOOM

🇲🇽🚆 <u>Rizo de Oro Bridge Opens in Chiapas</u>

Sheinbaum opened the Rizo de Oro steel-arch bridge in La Concordia, Chiapas: 2.308 billion pesos, 2 km long, more than 5,700 jobs during construction, and 300,000 people served, El Soberano reports. The trip between Tuxtla Gutiérrez and Frontera Comalapa drops from over five hours to about two and a half. Criminal threats in the Frailesca and Sierra regions halted the work more than once. It opened anyway.
banner: CHIAPAS: RIZO DE ORO BRIDGE OPENS

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Inés Gómez Mont: 2.45 Billion Pesos Through Ghost Companies</u>

Mexico's Attorney General Ernestina Godoy laid out the scheme: about 2.45 billion pesos in 2016–2017 contracts from Peña Nieto's federal prison agency (OADPRS) went to ghost companies issuing fake invoices, and the money allegedly landed in the personal bank accounts of TV host Inés Gómez Mont. She faces three federal arrest warrants, including for organized crime and money laundering. Extradition from the US for her and her husband, Víctor Manuel Álvarez Puga, is still pending.
banner: GÓMEZ MONT: 2.45B PESOS VIA GHOST FIRMS
